lesson.title: Gene therapy
lesson.scope: Explain how therapeutic genes can be delivered to target cells and evaluate limitations.
lesson.subtitle: 28 pages · original diagrams · written practice

screens.title: Fixing the Unfixable?
screens.html:
Fixing the Unfixable?

Imagine the Scenario

A child is born with a genetic mutation that prevents their body from making a vital enzyme.

Instead of treating the symptoms for the rest of their life, what if we could simply replace the broken instructions in their DNA?

screens.title: CORE CONCEPT
screens.html:
CORE CONCEPT

Defining Gene Therapy

Gene therapy is a technique that uses genes to treat or prevent disease by inserting a functional gene into a patient’s cells.

It aims to treat the underlying cause of a disorder rather than just managing it.

screens.title: Mechanisms of Action
screens.html:
Mechanisms of Action

There are three primary ways scientists use gene therapy to tackle genetic disorders:

Gene Augmentation: Replacing a mutated gene with a healthy copy.

Gene Inhibition: Inactivating a mutated gene that functions improperly.

Killing Cells: Inserting DNA into diseased cells to trigger cell death.

screens.title: The Challenge: Delivery
screens.html:
🔑

The Challenge: Delivery

DNA cannot simply be swallowed or injected like a pill. It is large, negatively charged, and easily broken down by the body.

To get the gene into the nucleus of a target cell, we need a vector (a vehicle).

Key point

Vectors are mostly derived from modified viruses, taking advantage of their natural ability to infect cells.

screens.title: Viral Vectors
screens.html:
Viral Vectors

Viruses are engineered to be safe by removing their ability to replicate and cause disease.

Common types include:

Retroviruses: Integrate DNA into the host genome.

Adenoviruses: DNA remains 'extra' (episomal) and isn't integrated.

screens.title: DELIVERY METHODS
screens.html:
DELIVERY METHODS

Direct Delivery (In Vivo)

In in vivo gene therapy, the vector is injected directly into the patient's body (e.g., into the bloodstream or an organ like the eye).

This is used when target cells cannot be easily removed from the patient.

screens.title: Cell-Based Delivery (Ex Vivo)
screens.html:
Cell-Based Delivery (Ex Vivo)

Extraction

Relevant cells (e.g., bone marrow) are removed from the patient.

Modification

Vectors carry the therapeutic gene into these cells in a laboratory.

Reintroduction

The modified, healthy cells are infused back into the patient.

screens.title: Choosing the Right Method
screens.html:
🔍

Choosing the Right Method

The choice between in vivo and ex vivo depends on the tissue type.

Blood and bone marrow disorders are often treated ex vivo, while eye or brain disorders require in vivo delivery.

Example

LCA (a form of blindness) is treated with a direct injection into the retina.

screens.title: In Vivo vs Ex Vivo
screens.html:
In Vivo vs Ex Vivo

Ex vivo gene therapy carries a lower risk of an immune reaction to the viral vector compared to in vivo therapy.

👍​

TRUE

👎​

FALSE

Now it's time to explain why...

screens.title: In Vivo vs Ex Vivo
screens.html:
In Vivo vs Ex Vivo

Ex vivo gene therapy carries a lower risk of an immune reaction to the viral vector compared to in vivo therapy.

👍​

Why is that?

a) Ex vivo therapy uses non-viral vectors which are naturally invisible to the immune system.

b) The vector is applied to cells in a lab, so the patient's immune system isn't directly exposed to the large dose of the virus.

screens.title: Target Diseases
screens.html:
Target Diseases

Gene therapy is most suitable for single-gene (monogenic) disorders.

Common targets include:

Cystic Fibrosis

Haemophilia

Huntington's Disease

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

screens.title: Treating Diabetes Mellitus
screens.html:
Treating Diabetes Mellitus

Current treatment for Type 1 Diabetes involves lifelong insulin injections. Gene therapy offers a permanent alternative.

Scientists aim to engineer non-pancreatic cells (like the liver) to produce and secrete insulin in response to blood glucose levels.

screens.title: Gene Therapy for Diabetes
screens.html:
Gene Therapy for Diabetes

The Goal

Insert a functional insulin gene into liver cells. The liver is an ideal target for 'moonlighting' as an insulin producer.

The Challenge

Control! Pancreatic cells adjust insulin instantly. Liver cells require a glucose-sensitive promoter to ensure the correct dose.

screens.title: CURRENT SUCCESS
screens.html:
CURRENT SUCCESS

Successes: The SCID Victory

SCID (the 'Boy in the Bubble' disease) was one of the first gene therapy successes.

Children without a functioning immune system have had their bone marrow cells modified ex vivo, allowing them to lead normal lives today.

screens.title: Limitations: Delivery Barriers
screens.html:
⚠️

Limitations: Delivery Barriers

Gene therapy is not yet a routine treatment due to several roadblocks:

Short-lived nature: If the gene doesn't integrate, it's lost when cells divide (problematic for skin or blood).

Watch out

Immune Response: The patient's immune system may attack the viral vector, causing dangerous inflammation.

screens.title: Limitations: Multigene Disorders
screens.html:
Limitations: Multigene Disorders

Most common diseases (heart disease, cancer, high blood pressure) are multigene.

Directing therapy at dozens of affected genes simultaneously is currently beyond our technical capability.

screens.title: Evaluating Limitations
screens.html:
Evaluating Limitations

Which of the following describes 'Insertional Mutagenesis'—a major risk of viral vectors?

1.

The virus loses the ability to carry the gene.

2.

The new gene integrates into and disrupts a healthy gene, potentially causing cancer.

3.

The patient's immune system destroys the virus before it reaches the cell.

4.

The gene is only expressed for a few days before disappearing.

Answers on the next slide...

screens.title: Is it Ethical?
screens.html:
Is it Ethical?

Gene therapy is currently limited to Somatic Cells (non-reproductive cells). This means the changes are not passed to the next generation.

Germline therapy (modifying eggs or sperm) is illegal in most countries, including Australia.

The Mechanism Summary

In gene therapy, a vector is used to deliver a functional gene. If this happens outside the body, it is called ex vivo delivery. screens.title: Gene Therapy Pros and Cons
screens.html:
🤯

Gene Therapy Pros and Cons

Successes

Curing previously fatal immune disorders (SCID).

Restoring vision in specific genetic blindness.

Reducing dependence on daily medication.

Limitations

Extremely high cost.

Risk of immune rejection.

Difficulty targeting internal organs effectively.

Fun fact

The world's most expensive drug, Hemgenix, is a one-time gene therapy for Haemophilia B costing roughly $3.5 million USD.

screens.title: Exam Prep: Ethical Evaluation
screens.html:
Exam Prep: Ethical Evaluation

Some argue gene therapy for diabetes is 'playing God', while others see it as a moral necessity to alleviate suffering. Evaluate using gene therapy for diabetes to improve quality of life.

screens.title: Exam Prep: Ethical Evaluation
screens.html:
Exam Prep: Ethical Evaluation

You might have said...

Improves quality of life by eliminating daily finger-pricks and injections.

Reduces long-term complication risks via steadier glucose control.

Ethically, it promotes beneficence by offering a potential cure.

Concerns remain regarding equity of access and unknown long-term effects.

✅​

screens.title: Summary & Next Steps
screens.html:
Summary & Next Steps

Gene therapy represents a shift from 'managing' to 'correcting' biology.

Key Takeaways:

Vectors (viruses) are the postmen of the gene world.

In vivo (inside) vs Ex vivo (outside).

Modern focus on monogenic diseases and diabetes.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Explain how gene augmentation may treat a disorder caused by a non-functional gene. Include one limitation.
steps: Identify a functional coding sequence and deliver it to suitable target cells using an appropriate vector or delivery system.
Expression of the added gene can provide a functional product and improve the relevant cell function.
Delivery may not reach enough cells, expression may be temporary, or immune and other adverse effects may occur.

bank.q: What does somatic gene therapy target?
o: Body cells other than the germline
bank.why: Somatic treatment changes body cells and is not intended to create inherited changes in offspring.

bank.q: What is a vector in gene therapy?
o: A delivery system for genetic material
bank.why: A vector carries therapeutic genetic material to target cells.

bank.q: Which is a challenge for gene therapy?
o: Delivering and expressing the material safely in enough target cells
Removing the need to identify the gene
Guaranteeing an identical response in every person
bank.why: Delivery, expression, immune responses and other safety issues can limit effectiveness.
